items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I’ve gotten to play with some of the greatest man. I mean that CD we did together... Bill Watrous

ctx.x: So there was some use in that thing there.

Some use there, just conduct yourself in a nice manner. But I’ve gotten to play with some of the greatest man. I mean that CD we did together, you had some of the greatest people on there — Bill Watrous, Jerome Richardson, Keter Betts, yourself.

items.title: Bill Watrous interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 26, 1999
items.q: I was talking with Wendell Brunious, a fabulous trumpet player, about that, how we have both gone through these stages.

ctx.x: The jazz music certainly was changing a lot in those times. Did you get into what was I guess called avant garde or free jazz at all?

I did for a while. Actually what I got into was a rock group called Eclipse. And in this group was Mike Lawrence, a very, very talented trumpet player and Dean Pratt who was a trumpet player who really wanted to play drums so he played drums, and this guy Allen Govan, who became my lead alto player in my big band after a while, and a bunch of us, and we literally wrote our own material. And it was, and the stuff we played, basically the group was sort of like Frank Zappa was what it was. I mean you talk about…

one until we scored a kid named Kim Milford, who became the singer and leader actor in the Rocky Horror Picture Show. He left us to go do that, and then we were in the lurch without a singer, and nothing happened, the group just came unglued, but we were really taking everything out. I mean I don’t think any of us played a chord tone in any of the solos that we played. Once in a while I will go way outside. I worked last weekend, I was in Delaware Water Gap, I worked a couple of couple of concerts with this high…
